messages.subject: Unsupported nodes ?
parts:
Hello All,
I am new to using BioGeoBEARS and I am wondering how unsupported nodes in the input tree affect the analysis. I assume the range estimate of the unsupported node shouldn't be used, but what is the impact on the geographic range estimate of nodes that are deep to the unsupported node?

I have not seen this addressed so I assume it is either not a problem or all users have perfectly supported trees (or I missed the discussion). Any input and insight would be greatly appreciated

Cheers

Elijah Wostl

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Unsupported nodes ?
parts:
Hi!  The short answer is that BioGeoBEARS (and Lagrange and any other comparative methods program that doesn't actively infer the phylogeny) are just taking whatever tree you give the program as The Correct Tree.  These programs don't know anything about node uncertainty, so they don't take it into account.

The typical "solution" to node uncertainty is to get a collection of trees, and run each one individually through the biogeography analysis, and then chose some method to summarize over the uncertainty in tree.  

I have...opinions on how this is often done in the literature.  I feel like often, I see "do lots of computation of dubious utility" privileged over "think carefully about what your question is and whether or not the tree uncertainty matters for this question, and if so how you will measure it and how you will display the results".

For example, in my humble opinion:

Strategy #1: Run DIVA on 50,000 trees from a Bayesian posterior analysis (using e.g. RASP), based on the idea that all of this furious effort somehow "accounts for uncertainty".  

Reality: 
- 50 trees would be as good as 50,000
- none of the uncertainty in tree will matter much if your model is a poor fit/badly misspecified, which the DIVA model almost always seems to be
- In the end most people just display the results averaged on one tree anyway (often an MCC summary tree), so what was the point of all of that effort again?

Strategy #2:
- Run the collection of BioGeoBEARS models on 50 (or even 10 or 5 or 3) trees from the Bayesian posterior
- Inspect the model comparisons for each run and see if the same model(s) are strongly supported despite the tree uncertainty
- Inspect the parts of the tree that are uncertain and see if the biogeographical history estimate varies very much
- If it doesn't, just pick one tree or a summary tree and use that in the paper
- If it does, display a few options, or tabulate the possible histories for key nodes -- or just say, in the paper, "the results are ambiguous" for those nodes
- Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping, run on each tree from a sample of 10 or 50, could be used to fully characterize the uncertainty in event counts, directionality, etc., due to both tree uncertainty and uncertainty in history estimate

I like strategy #2 way better.  But it will require some skill with writing for-loops in R and working with R tables, tree objects, the prt() function, etc. to collate the results across multiple analyses.

Cheers!
Nick
